findings.issue: Source: 'As when fair Juno’s lord flashes his lightning ... even so did Agamemnon heave many a heavy sigh.' Candidate splits the simile into a free-standing statement with an added 'sometimes' ('The husband of fair Hera sometimes flashes his lightning') followed by 'In the same way', so the as-when/so structure is lost and a word is added.
findings.fix: All the other princes of the Achaeans slept soundly through the night, but Agamemnon son of Atreus was troubled and could find no rest. As when the husband of fair Hera flashes his lightning as a sign of heavy rain, or hail, or a snowfall that turns the ground white, or else as a sign that he will open the wide jaws of hungry war, so Agamemnon heaved many a heavy sigh, for his soul trembled within him. When he looked out over the plain of Troy, he marveled at the many watchfires burning in front of Ilium, and at the sound of pipes and flutes and the hum of men. But when he turned toward the ships and the armies of the Achaeans, he tore his hair out by handfuls before Zeus on high, and groaned aloud, so uneasy was his soul. In the end he decided it was best to go at once to Nestor son of Neleus, and see whether the two of them could find some way to save the Achaeans from destruction. So he got up, put on his shirt, tied his sandals on his comely feet, threw over his shoulders the skin of a huge tawny lion—a skin that reached his feet—and took his spear in his hand.

findings.issue: Butler’s 'exploit the Trojans' is evidently a garble for 'explore/spy on'; candidate’s 'scout the Trojans' is a sensible reading.
Butler’s 'Will to the ships and will exploit them' is a garble (likely 'spy upon'); candidate’s 'spy them out' is a sensible reading.

Source 'the darkness of the flying night'; candidate 'the darkness of the fleeing night' is odd (night does not flee) and inconsistent with p40, which renders the same Butler phrase 'flying hours of darkness' as 'fleeting hours'.
findings.fix: Dolon answered, his legs shaking under him. “Hector lured me away from my better judgment with his empty, flattering promises. He said he would give me the horses of the noble son of Peleus and his chariot decked with bronze. He told me to go through the darkness of the fleeting night, get close to the enemy, and find out whether the ships are still guarded as before, or whether the Achaeans, now that we have beaten them, plan to flee and are neglecting their watches out of sheer exhaustion.”

findings.issue: Source: Rhesus’s horses are 'the finest and strongest that I have ever seen'; candidate says 'the finest and biggest', changing the quality named.
findings.fix: “I will tell you everything truthfully,” replied Dolon. “Toward the sea lie the Carians, the Paeonian bowmen, the Leleges, the Cauconians and the noble Pelasgi. The Lycians, the proud Mysians, the Phrygians and the Meonians have their place on the side toward Thymbra. But why ask about all this? If you want to find a way into the Trojan host, there are the Thracians, who have only just arrived. They lie apart from the others at the far end of the camp, and their king is Rhesus son of Eioneus. His horses are the finest and strongest I have ever seen. They are whiter than snow and swifter than any wind. His chariot is decked with silver and gold, and he has brought his marvelous golden armor, of the rarest workmanship. It is too splendid for any mortal man to wear and fit only for the gods. Now take me to the ships, or tie me up securely here until you come back and have tested my words to see whether they are false or true.”

findings.issue: Source: 'Ulysses hung them up aloft in honour of Minerva'; candidate 'Odysseus held them up high' changes the act from hanging up the spoils to holding them up (p40 then has him set them on a tamarisk tree).
findings.fix: Dolon was reaching for his beard to plead with him further, but Diomedes struck him with his sword in the middle of the neck and cut through both sinews, so that his head fell rolling in the dust while he was still speaking. They took the ferret-skin cap from his head, and the wolf skin, the bow and the long spear. Odysseus hung them up aloft in honor of Athena, goddess of plunder, and prayed, “Accept these, goddess. We give them to you before all the gods on Olympus. Now guide us further, to the horses and the sleeping place of the Thracians.”

findings.issue: Source 'honour to the Achaean name' is the same phrase rendered in p7 as 'honor of the Achaean name'; here it is 'glory of the Achaeans', inconsistent.
findings.fix: Odysseus answered, “Nestor son of Neleus, honor of the Achaean name, heaven, if it so wills, can give us even better horses than these, for the gods are far mightier than we are. But the horses you ask about have just come from Thrace. Diomedes killed their king along with the twelve bravest of his companions. Close by the ships we took a thirteenth man, a scout whom Hector and the other Trojans had sent to spy on our ships.”
